screens.title: Tools and Techniques for Threat Hunting
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how threat hunters combine logs, endpoint telemetry, and network metadata to find malicious activity that avoids alerts. We will connect three perspectives: centralized log collection with a SIEM for correlation and historical queries, endpoint visibility from EDR for process and memory-level investigation, and network-level data for packet and flow analysis. You will see concrete query examples used to search for suspicious logins, pivot from a SIEM result into an EDR investigation, and perform targeted network captures to confirm command-and-control behavior. I will also cover behavioral analytics and common pitfalls like insufficient logging and alert fatigue. A practical scenario guides you through writing conceptual SIEM and EDR queries to investigate lateral movement, so you can practice structured hunting. By the end you will understand which tool to use for which question, how to refine queries to reduce false positives, and why complete data visibility is the foundation of effective hunting. Think about one service you manage now and what logs you would need to answer a sudden unusual login — that's the starting point of proactive hunting.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Tools and Techniques
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Tools and Techniques for Threat Hunting

Learn the roles of SIEM, EDR, and network analysis, and how precise queries and visibility drive proactive detections.

Hunt: Observe → Query → Pivot
In this lesson
SIEM queries and correlation

Use historical logs and enrichment to find anomalous access patterns.

Coming up
EDR pivoting

Investigate process chains and memory activity on endpoints.

And also
Network and flow analysis

Capture packets or examine NetFlow to confirm C2 or exfiltration.

Explore Key Topics
SIEM
Centralize logs, enrich with geoip, and run historical queries to spot out-of-pattern access.
EDR
Endpoint telemetry exposes process creation, command lines, and memory activity for deep investigation.
Network
Packet captures and flow logs confirm protocol use, durations, and possible covert channels.
Visual Concept
Four-layer view
Logs → Endpoint → Network → Analytics
Why it matters
Gaps in any layer create blind spots. Combine layers for confident hunting and faster triage.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to practical threat hunting skills you will build. First, you will identify and describe common tools across network, endpoint, and log layers. That means knowing what SIEM, EDR, packet capture, and flow exporters can and cannot tell you. Second, you will learn to write and refine queries to search security logs and network data for suspicious behaviors, with real examples that filter noise and surface meaningful events. Third, you will understand how EDR enables endpoint-centric hunting: how to pivot from a network or SIEM alert to process chains, command lines, and memory indicators. Finally, you will apply behavioral analytics and anomaly-detection thinking to prioritize investigations. Each objective connects knowledge with a practical outcome: choosing the right tool, crafting the right query, investigating an endpoint, and focusing on anomalies that matter. We'll also emphasize data visibility and safety so your hunts avoid blind spots and unnecessary impact. As you progress, check off each competency by running the hands-on scenario and comparing your queries against expected outputs.

screens.title: Skills and Safety Goals
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond tool familiarity and query construction, you will learn safety and privacy practices that make hunting sustainable in production environments. This includes using copies of data or sandboxed analysis when possible, following change control when touching live systems, and being aware of data retention and regulatory constraints when viewing user activity. You will practice writing queries that are precise and progressively broadened — start narrow and expand only when needed to avoid alert fatigue. Another goal is to interpret EDR telemetry responsibly: not every dubious command-line string is an attack, and context matters. Finally, you will learn to articulate data visibility gaps and request improved logging or telemetry. That skill is essential because hunting without the right logs is guesswork. Each objective includes a verified milestone so you can measure readiness: writing targeted queries, performing controlled endpoint pivots, and documenting visibility gaps for engineering to fix.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Learning Objectives
Privacy-aware hunting
  • Use copies or sandboxed data when possible and avoid live changes without approval.
  • Limit queries to necessary fields and follow retention-policy constraints.
  • Document access and communicate with owners when user data is inspected.
Pro tip
Build reusable query templates that include safe defaults and time bounds to avoid sweeping queries.
Visibility reporting
  • Track which hosts and logs are missing command-line or process telemetry.
  • Request telemetry changes with examples that show why fields matter.
  • Prioritize logging improvements for critical systems first.
Outcome
You will be able to assess visibility gaps and propose targeted telemetry improvements with concrete examples.

screens.title: Data Visibility: The Foundation of Hunting
screens.narratorSegment: Data visibility is the extent to which an organization can collect, store, and access relevant security data across endpoints, servers, network devices, and applications. It is the foundational requirement for any effective hunt: you can only ask questions of data you have. For example, if process command-line arguments are not collected from endpoints, you cannot detect encoded PowerShell misuse or suspicious LOLBIN calls by searching for command-line patterns. A concrete example: a hunter looking for lateral movement needs successful login records, source host, destination host, and timestamps; if those keys are missing or aggregated out of context, the hunt will fail. A common misconception is that more data automatically improves hunting. In practice, unstructured or noise-heavy logs without enrichment produce alert fatigue; quality, relevant fields and proper retention windows matter more. To improve visibility, document required fields, instrument critical hosts with agents that capture process and network telemetry, and verify SIEM ingestion with small test events. Finally, think about privacy and retention: collect required fields, avoid storing unnecessary user data, and keep short, precise retention policies. What key logs would you request first for a business-critical database server?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Data Visibility
Definition

What visibility includes

  • Structured logs: timestamps, user, source host, destination host, event IDs.
  • Endpoint telemetry: process creation, command line, parent process, loaded modules.
  • Network data: packet captures, Zeek logs, NetFlow metadata.
  • Enrichment fields: geoip, asset tags, owner, criticality.
Misconception
More raw logs without key fields increases noise. Focus on collecting the right fields with context.
Concrete Example
To detect suspicious PowerShell execution, ensure the endpoint agent captures the process command line and parent process name. With these fields you can search for powerhsell.exe with encoded commands or unusual parent-child relationships.
Why it matters
Hunters can only validate hypotheses when fields and timestamps are precise and accessible.
Action
Audit telemetry coverage for critical hosts, request missing fields, and test ingestion with sample events.
Check your understanding
Name three required fields you would request to investigate a failed login followed by a successful login from an unusual IP.

screens.title: SIEM: Querying Logs and Enrichment
screens.narratorSegment: A Security Information and Event Management system centralizes logs and enables correlation across devices and time. The practical power of a SIEM is the ability to write focused queries that join raw events with enrichment data like geoip or asset tags. For example, a typical hunting pattern is to find successful logins to critical servers from sources outside expected geographies or during off-hours. The sample Splunk-like query shown in the visual searches for successful Windows logons to critical servers, enriches with geoip data, filters out domestic traffic, and counts occurrences over the last seven days. As a concrete example, this query can reveal an account appearing in multiple countries within a short window — a strong indicator of credential compromise. A common misconception is to run very broad queries that cover months of data; this produces huge result sets and many false positives. Instead, start with a tight time window and relevant hosts, then expand as needed. Practice refining where clauses and using stats to aggregate results. When a result looks suspicious, export the timestamp and host to pivot into EDR for process-level investigation. What would you change in the query to focus on only service accounts?

keyIdea.title: Queries + enrichment
keyIdea.text: Combine focused time windows, host filters, and enrichment like geoip to surface suspicious access patterns quickly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › SIEM Queries
Query Walkthrough

Search for suspicious logins

This query demonstrates enrichment and filtering to find successful Windows logins to critical servers originating outside the United States in the past seven days.
index=windows_events event_id=4624 (dest_host="critical_server_A" OR dest_host="critical_server_B") | lookup geoip client_ip AS src_ip | where geo_country != "United States" AND _time > relative_time(now(), "-7d") | stats count by _time, user, src_ip, geo_country | sort - count
Example output
Timestamps, user, source IP, and country counts to spot repeat occurrences from unusual locations.
Refinement tip
Add user role or asset tags to focus on service accounts or high-value systems only.
Supporting points
  • Use short windows to reduce noise and iterate outward if needed.
  • Enrich IPs with geoip or asset metadata to add context to raw events.
  • Aggregate with stats to surface users or IPs that repeat across hosts.
  • Pivot suspicious timestamps and hosts into EDR for endpoint validation.
Common mistake
Running month-long queries without filters creates too much data and hides meaningful signals.
Key Takeaway

Start narrow, enrich results, and aggregate to find repeat patterns that indicate compromise.

screens.title: EDR: Endpoint Telemetry and Pivoting
screens.narratorSegment: Endpoint Detection and Response systems provide the granular telemetry hunters need to reconstruct attacker actions on a host. EDR agents continuously collect events such as process creation, process parentage, command-line arguments, network connections, file writes, and module loads. The practical hunting pattern is to pivot from a SIEM result — for example, a suspicious login — into the EDR record for that host and examine the chain of process creations leading up to and following the event. A concrete example: a SIEM alert shows a login from a service account. The hunter pivots to the endpoint and queries for instances where Microsoft Word spawned PowerShell. If you find a winword. exe parent spawning powershell. exe with encoded commands, this strongly indicates a malicious document executing laterally. A common misconception is to treat all unusual commands as confirmed compromise; context like user activity, scheduled tasks, or maintenance scripts can appear similar. Validate by correlating timestamps, parent processes, and network connections. Finally, EDR queries often include vendor-specific syntax, but the logical fields remain the same: host_name, process_name, parent_process_name, command_line, and timestamp. How would you prioritize endpoints when several hosts show related suspicious activity?

keyIdea.title: EDR pivot pattern
keyIdea.text: Use EDR to reconstruct process chains and validate suspicious SIEM findings with command-line and parent-child context.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › EDR Pivoting
Endpoint Architecture

Telemetry you need

  • Process create events with parent and command line.
  • File write and module load events.
  • Memory access and suspicious injection indicators.
  • Network connections originating from processes.
Analogy
Think of EDR as the host's black box: it records the sequence of actions that let you reconstruct what happened and when.
Concrete scenario
A SIEM alert shows a service account login to DB_PROD_01 at 3 AM coming from WEB_APP_01. In the EDR console for WEB_APP_01, search for process creations around 2:50 to 3:10. Look for suspicious parents like winword.exe spawning powershell.exe or cmd.exe invoking credential-dumping tools.
What to verify
  • Timestamps align with the SIEM event.
  • Parent process is unusual for that host or user.
  • Command-line contains encoded or suspicious arguments.
  • Network connections to rare external destinations follow the process.
Key Takeaway

EDR lets you validate and enrich SIEM hypotheses by exposing the host-level activity that proves or disproves attacker behavior.

screens.title: EDR Query Patterns and TTPs
screens.narratorSegment: Hunters look for patterns of tactic, technique, and procedure rather than just filenames. EDR query patterns focus on relationships: who created which process, what command-line arguments were used, and whether a process accessed memory or loaded unusual modules. Common TTP searches include processes spawning uncommon children — for example, winword. exe spawning powershell. exe — attempts to access lsass. exe memory space indicating credential dumping, and execution of living-off-the-land binaries with suspicious arguments. A concrete EDR query example would search for PROCESS_CREATE where the parent is winword. exe and the child is powershell. exe. This pattern captures malicious documents that drop or execute script. A misconception is to rely solely on file hashes or names; modern attacks often use legitimate binaries with malicious arguments. Therefore, prioritize parent-child relationships and command line analysis. When you find a suspect event, collect the process tree, command lines, user context, and any subsequent network connections. That collected evidence allows you to determine if the activity was scripted admin work or an adversary operating in the environment. EDR Query Patterns and TTPs means search for parent-child relationships, command-line anomalies, and memory access rather than only file names or hashes.. In practical terms, searches that reveal process abuse and credential access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › EDR Patterns
EDR Query Example

Parent-child process search

A conceptual EDR query that hunts for Word spawning PowerShell, a common malicious document pattern. Vendor syntax varies, but fields are consistent.
PROCESS_CREATE where ParentProcessName = "winword.exe" and ProcessName = "powershell.exe"
Why this helps
It surfaces cases where a document invoked scripting, bypassing static file checks.
Misconception
Not every powerhsell.exe instance is malicious; check command-line and parentage to avoid false positives.
Supporting searches and checks
  • Search for lsass.exe memory access or suspicious credential dumping indicators.
  • Look for LOLBINs like certutil or bitsadmin with unusual arguments.
  • Inspect module loads and file writes immediately after suspicious process creation.
Key Takeaway

Focus on behavior and relationships. Use command-line and parent context to separate admin activity from malicious chains.

screens.title: Network Analysis: Packets vs Flows
screens.narratorSegment: Network-level hunting uses two complementary data sources: packet captures and flow metadata. Packet capture tools like tcpdump and Wireshark record full packet payloads and are indispensable when you need to inspect actual protocol contents to confirm data exfiltration or command-and-control. For example, a targeted capture filtered for a host and external IP can reveal HTTP POSTs containing uploaded data or specific C2 payloads. In contrast, NetFlow or IPFIX provides lightweight metadata about conversations — who talked to whom, on which port, for how long, and how many bytes. Flows are excellent for spotting long-lived, low-volume connections consistent with covert channels. Zeek sits in between: it inspects packets and emits structured logs (DNS, HTTP, connection records) that are more searchable in a SIEM. A common misconception is that flows are enough to prove payload content; they are not. Use flows to prioritize targets for packet capture, then confirm with tcpdump or Wireshark. In practice, maintain short targeted captures and long-term flow logging so you can triage efficiently without storing massive packet archives. How would you use a flow anomaly to trigger a packet capture?

keyIdea.title: Flows narrow, packets confirm
keyIdea.text: Use NetFlow to detect anomalies and packet captures or Zeek logs to confirm protocol-level details and payloads.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Network Analysis
Tool comparison
Packet capture (tcpdump / Wireshark)
Full packet contents for protocol inspection and payload validation. Use for targeted, time-bound captures to avoid storing large volumes.
Flow data (NetFlow / IPFIX)
Metadata about conversations: source, destination, port, duration, and size. Good for long-term anomaly detection and prioritization.
Zeek
Performs deep inspection and emits structured logs for DNS, HTTP, and connections that are easy to search in a SIEM.
Practical workflow
  1. Use NetFlow to find unusual long-lived or low-volume external connections.
  2. Identify the internal host and external IP from the flow record.
  3. Trigger a targeted packet capture for that host and IP to confirm payload or protocol misuse.
Key takeaway
Flows help you prioritize. Packets and Zeek logs give the evidence you need to confirm exfiltration or C2.

screens.title: Behavioral Analytics and Anomaly Detection
screens.narratorSegment: Behavioral analytics builds baselines of normal user and system activity and flags deviations as anomalous. This is often implemented inside SIEM, EDR, or dedicated UEBA systems. The key advantage is that anomalies can surface stealthy activity that does not match known indicators of compromise. For example, if a user normally accesses resources from one subnet and suddenly authenticates from a foreign country and immediately requests new sensitive files, the sequence of deviations becomes a high-priority lead even without a classic IoC. A common misconception is that anomalies are automatically malicious; instead, they are signals that require context and validation. Hunters should combine anomaly alerts with raw logs and endpoint telemetry to confirm intent: check timestamps, device posture, and whether automation or scheduled jobs could explain the behavior. Practically, use behavioral outputs to focus hunting resources on the riskiest entities, then apply SIEM and EDR queries to gather evidence. Always tune baselines to business patterns to reduce false positives and maintain analyst trust. How would you validate an anomaly that flags elevated file access by a user during a maintenance window?

keyIdea.text: Use behavioral deviations to prioritize hunts, but always validate with context and endpoint evidence before concluding compromise.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Behavioral Analytics
Definition

Baseline and deviation

Baselines define normal ranges for logins, access patterns, and process activity. Anomalies are deviations from those baselines and help prioritize investigations when signature-based detections miss novel behavior.

Example
A UEBA alert flags a user accessing sensitive files from an overseas IP outside normal hours. This sequence, combined with a login anomaly, raises priority.
Investigation steps
  1. Verify the anomaly against asset tags and scheduled maintenance windows.
  2. Pivot to SIEM logs for authentication details and source IP history.
  3. Use EDR to inspect process activity and network connections for the endpoint involved.
Key Takeaway
Anomalies should focus your hunting effort. Always validate with logs and endpoint telemetry before escalating.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safe Hunting Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Threat hunting can be undermined by two recurring mistakes: insufficient data visibility and overly broad queries that cause alert fatigue. Insufficient visibility usually means missing fields like command-line arguments, parent process names, or asset tags; without those, conclusions are tentative. Overly broad queries produce too many false positives and diminish trust in hunting outputs. To mitigate these problems, adopt a practice of progressive query expansion: start with a focused hypothesis, run a narrow search, and expand the scope if the results justify it. Safety is also critical: prefer working on copies of data or in non-production environments where possible, and if you must analyze or capture live traffic, follow change control and communicate with system owners. Respect privacy by limiting fields and documenting access reasoning. A practical workflow: form a hypothesis, identify required telemetry, run a tight query, pivot to endpoint and network for confirmation, then document findings and recommended telemetry improvements. A common misconception is that hunters must always run live captures. Instead, use flows and Zeek logs to triage, and capture packets only when they are necessary to confirm payloads.

Safety is also critical: prefer working on copies of data or in non-production environments where possible, and if you must analyze or capture live traffic, follow change control and communicate with system owners. Respect privacy by limiting fields and documenting access reasoning. A practical workflow: form a hypothesis, identify required telemetry, run a tight query, pivot to endpoint and network for confirmation, then document findings and recommended telemetry improvements. A common misconception is that hunters must always run live captures. Instead, use flows and Zeek logs to triage, and capture packets only when they are necessary to confirm payloads.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Safe Hunting
Progressive query workflow
  1. Form a specific hypothesis (e.g., unusual service account login).
  2. Identify required fields and confirm telemetry exists.
  3. Run a narrow, time-bounded query and inspect top results.
  4. Pivot to EDR and network logs for corroboration before escalating.
Safety checklist
  • Prefer non-production data or copies when possible.
  • Limit fields and document access for privacy compliance.
  • Coordinate captures with owners and follow change control.
Common Mistakes
  • Blindly broad queries that return millions of rows.
  • Assuming every anomaly equals compromise without context.
  • Failing to collect command-line or parent process fields.
Key Takeaway
Hunt methodically, validate with multiple data sources, and protect systems and privacy while investigating.

screens.title: Scenario: SIEM Query for Suspicious Service Account Login
screens.narratorSegment: We will work through a practical SIEM query for the hands-on scenario: a suspicious login by svc_web_app to DB_PROD_01 at 3 AM when the account normally accesses WEB_APP_01. The hunting goal is to find all login attempts by that service account to any host other than WEB_APP_01 within the last 24 hours. A well-formed query limits the time window, filters the user and excluded host, and returns essential fields for triage. The output should show timestamp, user, source host, destination host, and event ID so you can quickly spot when and where the account accessed unexpected hosts. A common mistake is omitting the time bound and returning extraneous historical events. After running the query, take any suspicious _time and dest_host pairs and pivot to EDR for process and command-line investigation on the source host. This two-step approach narrows evidence collection and reduces load on both SIEM and EDR systems. Try running the query and then documenting one example row you would pivot on and why. keyIdea.text: Form time-bounded, user- and host-filtered queries that return focused fields for fast triage and pivoting.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › SIEM Scenario
Task

Find svc_web_app logins to non-standard hosts

The expected output fields are _time, user, src_host, dest_host, and event_id. Use a 24-hour window to limit noise.

index=windows_events event_id=4624 user="svc_web_app" dest_host!="WEB_APP_01" _time > relative_time(now(), "-24h") | table _time, user, src_host, dest_host, event_id
Expected result
A small table of login events that show unexpected destinations, ready for pivoting into EDR or network logs.
Investigation next steps
  • Take suspicious rows and note _time and src_host to pivot to EDR.
  • On the source host, search for process creation events +/- 20 minutes around the login.
  • Look for parent-child anomalies, LOLBIN usage, and outbound connections that may indicate pivoting.
Check your understanding
If the SIEM returns multiple dest_host values for the same _time and user, what pivot would you run first and why?

screens.title: Scenario: EDR Query for Process Creation on WEB_APP_01
screens.narratorSegment: After identifying WEB_APP_01 as the source host in the SIEM, the next step is to query the EDR for process creation events during a focused time window around the suspicious login — for example, 2:50 AM to 3:10 AM. The goal is to find processes that indicate an attacker gained control of the web app and pivoted to the database server. Look for parent processes like winword. exe, cmd. exe, or services spawning PowerShell, psexec, or wmic. Also search for command-line strings that contain credential dumping commands or lateral movement tools. The conceptual EDR query included in the visual is vendor-agnostic: it restricts by host and timestamp range and checks for a set of suspicious process names or command-line patterns. If you locate a matching event, capture the _time, process_name, command_line, parent_process_name, and user, then cross-reference network logs for connections that coincide with that process. This combined evidence will help distinguish routine maintenance from malicious activity. Scenario: EDR Query for Process Creation on WEB_APP_01 means run time-bound, host-focused searches for suspicious process names and command-line patterns, then correlate with network evidence.. In practical terms, investigate process execution around the suspicious login time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Run time-bound, host-focused searches for suspicious process names and command-line patterns, then correlate with network evidence.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › EDR Scenario
EDR Query (Conceptual)

Search for suspicious process creation events

Adjust vendor syntax as needed. Target the host WEB_APP_01 and the narrow time window around the login.
host_name="WEB_APP_01" AND event_time BETWEEN "2023-10-26T02:50:00Z" AND "2023-10-26T03:10:00Z" AND ( process_name IN ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe", "wmic.exe", "psexec.exe") OR command_line CONTAINS "Invoke-Mimikatz" OR command_line CONTAINS "net user" OR command_line CONTAINS "whoami" ) | select event_time, process_name, command_line, parent_process_name, user
Why this helps
It surfaces suspicious process activity and command-line evidence you can use to confirm whether the web host was used to pivot to the database.
Follow-up
  • If you find suspicious processes, collect the entire process tree and any dropped artifacts.
  • Correlate process timestamps with network logs to find outbound connections or database access attempts.
  • Document findings and recommend containment steps if evidence supports compromise.
Key Takeaway
Time-bound, host-focused EDR searches reveal the process-level evidence needed to confirm or refute a suspected compromise.

screens.title: Combining SIEM, EDR, and Network Data
screens.narratorSegment: Successful hunting combines SIEM, EDR, and network insights in a deliberate workflow. Start with a SIEM hypothesis or anomaly that prioritizes an investigation. Use the SIEM to obtain timestamps, users, and host identifiers. Next, pivot into EDR for host-centric evidence: process trees, command lines, and memory events. If process activity shows network connections or suspicious file exfiltration, consult flow records or Zeek logs to understand conversation patterns. If flows are suspicious, capture packets for payload inspection with tcpdump or Wireshark to confirm data exfiltration or C2 commands. A concrete example: SIEM shows an unusual login; EDR reveals winword spawning PowerShell with encoded commands; Zeek shows DNS requests to a rare domain from that host; a targeted packet capture confirms tunneling in DNS. A common misconception is assuming a single source will provide all answers; instead, combine sources and keep each query tight. Document each step, preserve timestamps, and prepare to report findings with artifact references. Which evidence would you include in an executive summary versus a technical containment ticket? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Integration Workflow
Workflow Steps
  1. Detect: SIEM query or UEBA anomaly identifies an event or user of interest.
  2. Pivot: Use SIEM fields to pivot to EDR for process and memory evidence.
  3. Corroborate: Check network flows or Zeek logs for unusual destinations or protocols.
  4. Confirm: Take a targeted packet capture only when necessary to inspect payloads.
  5. Document: Save timestamps, artifacts, and recommended containment steps.
Scenario snapshot
Example chain: SIEM alarm → EDR shows Document→PowerShell → Zeek shows rare DNS → Packet capture reveals DNS tunneling. Each layer adds a piece of the story and increases confidence before containment.
Key Takeaway
Layered evidence reduces uncertainty. Use tight queries and cross-source correlation to build a defensible incident narrative.

SIEM
Central log aggregation and correlation platform for historical queries and enrichment.
EDR
Endpoint telemetry platform capturing process, memory, and file activity for host investigations.

Quick summary

Use SIEM to find leads, EDR to validate behavior, and network tools to confirm communications. Improve telemetry and tune queries for sustainable, accurate hunting.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how threat hunters combine logs, endpoint telemetry, and network metadata to find malicious activity that avoids alerts. We will connect three perspectives: centralized log collection with a SIEM for correlation and historical queries, endpoint visibility from EDR for process and memory-level investigation, and network-level data for packet and flow analysis. You will see concrete query examples used to search for suspicious logins, pivot from a SIEM result into an EDR investigation, and perform targeted network captures to confirm command-and-control behavior. I will also cover behavioral analytics and common pitfalls like insufficient logging and alert fatigue. A practical scenario guides you through writing conceptual SIEM and EDR queries to investigate lateral movement, so you can practice structured hunting. By the end you will understand which tool to use for which question, how to refine queries to reduce false positives, and why complete data visibility is the foundation of effective hunting. Think about one service you manage now and what logs you would need to answer a sudden unusual login — that's the starting point of proactive hunting.

These four objectives map to practical threat hunting skills you will build. First, you will identify and describe common tools across network, endpoint, and log layers. That means knowing what SIEM, EDR, packet capture, and flow exporters can and cannot tell you. Second, you will learn to write and refine queries to search security logs and network data for suspicious behaviors, with real examples that filter noise and surface meaningful events. Third, you will understand how EDR enables endpoint-centric hunting: how to pivot from a network or SIEM alert to process chains, command lines, and memory indicators. Finally, you will apply behavioral analytics and anomaly-detection thinking to prioritize investigations. Each objective connects knowledge with a practical outcome: choosing the right tool, crafting the right query, investigating an endpoint, and focusing on anomalies that matter. We'll also emphasize data visibility and safety so your hunts avoid blind spots and unnecessary impact. As you progress, check off each competency by running the hands-on scenario and comparing your queries against expected outputs.

Beyond tool familiarity and query construction, you will learn safety and privacy practices that make hunting sustainable in production environments. This includes using copies of data or sandboxed analysis when possible, following change control when touching live systems, and being aware of data retention and regulatory constraints when viewing user activity. You will practice writing queries that are precise and progressively broadened — start narrow and expand only when needed to avoid alert fatigue. Another goal is to interpret EDR telemetry responsibly: not every dubious command-line string is an attack, and context matters. Finally, you will learn to articulate data visibility gaps and request improved logging or telemetry. That skill is essential because hunting without the right logs is guesswork. Each objective includes a verified milestone so you can measure readiness: writing targeted queries, performing controlled endpoint pivots, and documenting visibility gaps for engineering to fix.

Data visibility is the extent to which an organization can collect, store, and access relevant security data across endpoints, servers, network devices, and applications. It is the foundational requirement for any effective hunt: you can only ask questions of data you have. For example, if process command-line arguments are not collected from endpoints, you cannot detect encoded PowerShell misuse or suspicious LOLBIN calls by searching for command-line patterns. A concrete example: a hunter looking for lateral movement needs successful login records, source host, destination host, and timestamps; if those keys are missing or aggregated out of context, the hunt will fail. A common misconception is that more data automatically improves hunting. In practice, unstructured or noise-heavy logs without enrichment produce alert fatigue; quality, relevant fields and proper retention windows matter more. To improve visibility, document required fields, instrument critical hosts with agents that capture process and network telemetry, and verify SIEM ingestion with small test events. Finally, think about privacy and retention: collect required fields, avoid storing unnecessary user data, and keep short, precise retention policies. What key logs would you request first for a business-critical database server?

A Security Information and Event Management system centralizes logs and enables correlation across devices and time. The practical power of a SIEM is the ability to write focused queries that join raw events with enrichment data like geoip or asset tags. For example, a typical hunting pattern is to find successful logins to critical servers from sources outside expected geographies or during off-hours. The sample Splunk-like query shown in the visual searches for successful Windows logons to critical servers, enriches with geoip data, filters out domestic traffic, and counts occurrences over the last seven days. As a concrete example, this query can reveal an account appearing in multiple countries within a short window — a strong indicator of credential compromise. A common misconception is to run very broad queries that cover months of data; this produces huge result sets and many false positives. Instead, start with a tight time window and relevant hosts, then expand as needed. Practice refining where clauses and using stats to aggregate results. When a result looks suspicious, export the timestamp and host to pivot into EDR for process-level investigation. What would you change in the query to focus on only service accounts?

Endpoint Detection and Response systems provide the granular telemetry hunters need to reconstruct attacker actions on a host. EDR agents continuously collect events such as process creation, process parentage, command-line arguments, network connections, file writes, and module loads. The practical hunting pattern is to pivot from a SIEM result — for example, a suspicious login — into the EDR record for that host and examine the chain of process creations leading up to and following the event. A concrete example: a SIEM alert shows a login from a service account. The hunter pivots to the endpoint and queries for instances where Microsoft Word spawned PowerShell. If you find a winword. exe parent spawning powershell. exe with encoded commands, this strongly indicates a malicious document executing laterally. A common misconception is to treat all unusual commands as confirmed compromise; context like user activity, scheduled tasks, or maintenance scripts can appear similar. Validate by correlating timestamps, parent processes, and network connections. Finally, EDR queries often include vendor-specific syntax, but the logical fields remain the same: host_name, process_name, parent_process_name, command_line, and timestamp. How would you prioritize endpoints when several hosts show related suspicious activity?

Hunters look for patterns of tactic, technique, and procedure rather than just filenames. EDR query patterns focus on relationships: who created which process, what command-line arguments were used, and whether a process accessed memory or loaded unusual modules. Common TTP searches include processes spawning uncommon children — for example, winword. exe spawning powershell. exe — attempts to access lsass. exe memory space indicating credential dumping, and execution of living-off-the-land binaries with suspicious arguments. A concrete EDR query example would search for PROCESS_CREATE where the parent is winword. exe and the child is powershell. exe. This pattern captures malicious documents that drop or execute script. A misconception is to rely solely on file hashes or names; modern attacks often use legitimate binaries with malicious arguments. Therefore, prioritize parent-child relationships and command line analysis. When you find a suspect event, collect the process tree, command lines, user context, and any subsequent network connections. That collected evidence allows you to determine if the activity was scripted admin work or an adversary operating in the environment. EDR Query Patterns and TTPs means search for parent-child relationships, command-line anomalies, and memory access rather than only file names or hashes.. In practical terms, searches that reveal process abuse and credential access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network-level hunting uses two complementary data sources: packet captures and flow metadata. Packet capture tools like tcpdump and Wireshark record full packet payloads and are indispensable when you need to inspect actual protocol contents to confirm data exfiltration or command-and-control. For example, a targeted capture filtered for a host and external IP can reveal HTTP POSTs containing uploaded data or specific C2 payloads. In contrast, NetFlow or IPFIX provides lightweight metadata about conversations — who talked to whom, on which port, for how long, and how many bytes. Flows are excellent for spotting long-lived, low-volume connections consistent with covert channels. Zeek sits in between: it inspects packets and emits structured logs (DNS, HTTP, connection records) that are more searchable in a SIEM. A common misconception is that flows are enough to prove payload content; they are not. Use flows to prioritize targets for packet capture, then confirm with tcpdump or Wireshark. In practice, maintain short targeted captures and long-term flow logging so you can triage efficiently without storing massive packet archives. How would you use a flow anomaly to trigger a packet capture?

Behavioral analytics builds baselines of normal user and system activity and flags deviations as anomalous. This is often implemented inside SIEM, EDR, or dedicated UEBA systems. The key advantage is that anomalies can surface stealthy activity that does not match known indicators of compromise. For example, if a user normally accesses resources from one subnet and suddenly authenticates from a foreign country and immediately requests new sensitive files, the sequence of deviations becomes a high-priority lead even without a classic IoC. A common misconception is that anomalies are automatically malicious; instead, they are signals that require context and validation. Hunters should combine anomaly alerts with raw logs and endpoint telemetry to confirm intent: check timestamps, device posture, and whether automation or scheduled jobs could explain the behavior. Practically, use behavioral outputs to focus hunting resources on the riskiest entities, then apply SIEM and EDR queries to gather evidence. Always tune baselines to business patterns to reduce false positives and maintain analyst trust. How would you validate an anomaly that flags elevated file access by a user during a maintenance window?

Threat hunting can be undermined by two recurring mistakes: insufficient data visibility and overly broad queries that cause alert fatigue. Insufficient visibility usually means missing fields like command-line arguments, parent process names, or asset tags; without those, conclusions are tentative. Overly broad queries produce too many false positives and diminish trust in hunting outputs. To mitigate these problems, adopt a practice of progressive query expansion: start with a focused hypothesis, run a narrow search, and expand the scope if the results justify it. Safety is also critical: prefer working on copies of data or in non-production environments where possible, and if you must analyze or capture live traffic, follow change control and communicate with system owners. Respect privacy by limiting fields and documenting access reasoning. A practical workflow: form a hypothesis, identify required telemetry, run a tight query, pivot to endpoint and network for confirmation, then document findings and recommended telemetry improvements. A common misconception is that hunters must always run live captures. Instead, use flows and Zeek logs to triage, and capture packets only when they are necessary to confirm payloads.
